item.title: Endings Can Be Unbearable to Renewing
item.description:
Resilience

Endings Can Be Unbearable to Renewing

Personal Perspective: Responding to life's inevitable endings.

Posted August 19, 2026

For most people, moving on after a central part of their lives ends may be sad, but it isn’t usually devastating. The end of a relationship, a job, or a home can be challenging; you don’t know what’s next or how your life will reconfigure. Some people, however, particularly those who’ve suffered difficult early losses, may fear that their lives won’t reconfigure. For them, endings of any sort can seem ominous. I know. I have that person. Ending a seven-year live-in love relationship in my thirties left me with the confusing combination of relief, as if landing on the far shore of a river I wasn’t sure I could swim across, and dread that I’d landed in a place so foreign I’d be lost forever.

It took me a year, but I did recover from that breakup and settled into a happier ongoing romance. But it was harder still to recover from an ending I didn’t want, like the one I faced after being “terminated” from my first big teaching job. The morning after I’d gathered a couple of thousand people to hear Gloria Steinem, whose feminism the college administration spurned at that time, I was told I was too political and given the boot. Many years later, it’s still so painful; I wonder if I’ve ever fully recovered.

Even Minor Endings Can Feel Overwhelming

Okay, these two endings would count as big events in anyone’s life, but for those of us who have this sensitivity, far less significant endings can also feel shattering. I used to start my day with a morning run until I injured my foot so badly that I could only hobble a block or two at most. For a person in constant motion, immobility was agonizing. Disorienting. Yet even I was aware my reaction was disproportionately strong. When I complained to my therapist about my sport going kaput, she said, as if talking to a second grader, “You’ll find another.” After months of failed treatments, when I found myself contemplating suicide, I took up meditation. It gave me a whole new outlook. Now I could see how endings left space to cultivate another part of myself, which I did again after the right surgeon resolved my foot problem. Since running was still out, I started wandering up trails near where I lived instead. Eventually, wandering became hiking, a passion more rewarding to me than running ever was, a deep engagement with mountains and myself.

The very insignificance of this ending is what, on reflection, alerted me to the drama of my responses to the endings of things. I could track how my extreme and negative reaction morphed into a positive, even transformative one. How when endings trigger you as this one did me, slicing through your heart or burrowing into your core, they can leave you so raw and disturbed that you’re forced to find your way forward using deeper, more intuitive parts of yourselves. That’s surely what brought me to meditation and later, to hiking, both of which I still do, with dedication. And while that’s a good thing, it also raised the question: if endings are the portal to reinvention, inspiring resilience and flexibility, what makes them so hard for some of us to tolerate?

This is where psychoanalytic thinking comes into play, especially for people who’ve had those difficult early losses. Losses are pretty common in childhood. We have only to think of when parents divorce, a grandparent dies, or a child has to move away from their familiar home and friends. It doesn’t have to be a tragedy. If parents handle loss well, comforting their children, making them feel secure, and acknowledging their feelings, all’s generally well. If not, however, it’s worth knowing what you can about that childhood experience, even if you have to talk with your siblings or interview a couple of relatives to get the details. Knowing what happened then can make you aware of why a particular ending feels manageable, and another unmoors you.

The Role of Early Loss

I think it's easy to understand how, when facing an ending, the parents themselves might be inconsolable, too destabilized to offer their children a strong enough sense of security. Then, left on their own to deal with that ending before they’re equipped to handle it, children can feel that life as they know it is falling apart, or even that they are falling apart. These primitive fears might reemerge in adult life when an ending has stirred memories of earlier, often unconscious ones. They can shadow life’s inevitable closures. Luckily, awareness can calm them. Just knowing why you’re reacting can bring perspective and a sense of control to a chaotic time. It can signal the need for extra support, like meditation, therapy, or a visit with a beloved aunt. It can calm those primitive fears, allowing you to experience the ending for what it is, not what it was in childhood.

Putting whatever ending has arisen in the larger context of your life, beginning with any similar ending you may have had to face in childhood, can reveal how much past emotion you’re bringing to a current situation. It may illustrate how time moves us forward into the next iteration of ourselves, collecting new people, places, and projects even as it leaves others behind. It may eventually prove a good thing, an enriching one, not the corrosive disruption it was so long ago.

item.title: Diagnosing Death in the ICU: The Moment Time Stands Still
item.description:
Neuroscience

Diagnosing Death in the ICU: The Moment Time Stands Still

The one time in medicine that demands absolute certainty.

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Despite advanced neurotechnology, there's one very human step in the diagnosis of death in the ICU.
  • Diagnosing brain death entails three rigorous criteria, all of which must be met without question.
  • The exact moment of death is often arbitrary, but extremely meaningful to loved ones.

The longest ten minutes of my life are those I spend in perfect stillness and silence in the final throes of the brain death examination.

A young woman had been admitted after a highway crash, extricated after a long two hours from twisted metal that had crushed the car roof and doors. Her pupils were fixed and dilated when she arrived. She had been intubated in the field by EMS, lips and face blue, not able to breathe on her own. We cared for her bruised body gently, but her only life-threatening injury was bleeding and swelling in her brain, compressing her brainstem—our seat of life.

We tested her neurological function repeatedly for two days, for any sign of brainstem function—for any sign of life.

Source: photo by Stephen Andrews on Unsplash

We found none. It was my job to carefully take her through the rigorous criteria we would need to pronounce her brain dead, while her heart was still beating steadily and her limbs were pale pink and warm.

Those ten minutes were mine with her. My residents were in the room, along with two medical students, her nurse, and respiratory therapist. Her mom waited just outside the door. We took her off the ventilator, which was regularly pushing air into her lungs, but still passively supplied oxygen into her lungs, to see if she would breathe on her own.

I stood by her side, my eyes never leaving her chest, watching for a breath, just a small intake or rise that would indicate her lower brainstem function still had survived and still was doing its job to literally breathe life into her.

Her chest never moved.

There are two definitions of death, as established by The Uniform Determination of Death Act, accepted by most states:

  • irreversible cessation of cardiac and respiratory function, or
  • irreversible loss of function of the entire brain (brain death)

In our Neuro ICU we primarily diagnose brain death. In the United States brain death requires three criteria, rigorously assessed:

  • coma (and a reason for coma, such as anoxia (lack of oxygen) or cerebral bleeding)
  • loss of brainstem reflexes, “brainstem areflexia” (the brainstem controls consciousness and the activities that make us alive: blood pressure, heart rate, respiration)
  • loss of the ability to breathe spontaneously, tested by strict protocol in the Apnea Test for brain death
article continues after advertisement

A person must meet all three criteria, without question, to be declared brain dead. No one who meets these testing criteria for brain death has ever recovered—not one person.

When We Stop the Clock

This is a time in medicine where we simply cannot be wrong. Visibly watching for a small intake of breath is important, but not enough. We already knew that the parts of her brainstem above the medulla, which controlled pupillary response, reflexive swallowing and coughing, eye movements and motor function, were no longer viable.

Brain death in the U.S. requires death of the entire brain. We still needed proof that the medulla, in the lowest part of the brainstem, where respiration is controlled, was no longer functioning. So, we sent an arterial blood gas (which measures oxygen, pH and carbon dioxide in the blood), while the patient was off the ventilator. The blood gas gives us a specific rise in carbon dioxide, enough to trigger respirations in a living person. Carbon dioxide in the blood rises in a person who is not exhaling air and it’s a powerful trigger for the brain to initiate breath. If that target carbon dioxide is met, and the person still does not breathe, they are dead.

The precise moment of death, which we record for family and write in the medical chart, is the minute that blood gas returns with the specified required rise in carbon dioxide. Usually, a respiratory therapist will put the result in my hands for me to read the numbers out loud.

Source: photo by Kevin Andre on Unsplash

To us, that moment seems arbitrary, a minute in time when we know our patient had died before, but we don’t know exactly when. But to our patients’ families, that exact moment is very meaningful: 7:06 PM. Those numbers will often be engraved on a pendant or memorialized in a tattoo. Our patient’s boyfriend told us he would do just that; get a tattoo with her first name and 7:06 on his shoulder.

That moment, when the clock stops, signaling the end of one life, will live on in the lives of those who loved her.

item.title: How to Help Rural Victims of Domestic Violence
item.description:
Domestic Violence

How to Help Rural Victims of Domestic Violence

Addressing the psychology of domestic abuse in small towns

Posted August 19, 2026

Key points
  • Domestic violence detection is easier where population density involves frequent interaction.
  • In remote areas, unfamiliarity with such violence may complicate adequate risk assessment.
  • Small town dynamics present confidentiality concerns.
  • Isolated areas often lack infrastructure to facilitate victim services.

Domestic violence is a worldwide invisible epidemic, whether we “see” it or not. Detection is often easier in urban areas where population density involves more personal interaction than in rural or remote areas where abuse often flies under the radar. But with situational awareness and specialized knowledge of what to look for and where to look, it can more easily be identified and addressed.

Source: Image by Jose Antonio Alba from Pixabay

Remote Control: Identifying Intimate Partner Violence in Rural, Isolated Areas

Joakim Petersson and Anna-Karin Larsson (2025) investigated the experiences of social workers in identifying and assessing risks for intimate partner violence (IPV) in rural and remote areas.[i] Conducting 13 focus group interviews with 38 social workers from 17 rural and remote municipalities in Sweden, they identified three themes: challenges identifying IPV, different levels of expertise with risk assessment, and practical utility of available risk assessment tools. They further found that unfamiliarity with risk assessment was partially due to unfamiliarity with IPV, because cases were rarely identified.

Petersson and Larsson recognize that social workers in rural and remote areas face a wider range of social problems than workers in urban areas. Rural areas have fewer community resources and fewer staff. This makes it more difficult to gain sufficient knowledge, experience, and expertise within different areas of social welfare. Also, sparsely populated areas present unique spatial and social contexts that are susceptible to practical and socio-cultural constraints that negatively affect both victims' ability to seek support and professionals' ability to provide it.

Survivors Need Social Support

Petersson and Larsson acknowledge that victims request social services for reasons other than abuse, such as assistance with finances or housing. Accordingly, they recognize that to detect partner violence, social service professionals should be asking the right questions. They note what many in the field recognize instinctively: without sufficient training in screening, providers do not know what to ask, or what services are available. Intimate partner violence training should thus include methods of raising awareness of what other providers offer, such as healthcare or law enforcement services.

Petersson and Larsson also note that social workers who perform risk assessments should understand the link between intimate partner violence and violence risk—expertise unfortunately often limited to only a select few. Staff turnover in social services also affects this small group of trained workers.

Small Communities Preclude Anonymity

Complicating reporting rates is that many community members, including victims, perpetrators, and even family members, consider domestic violence to be a private matter. Petersson and Larsson note that this unique socio-cultural context of informal control and wanting to keep this private makes victims reluctant to disclose their abuse. They note that even entering the premises of a local social service center can create stigma, raising suspicion and questions from other community members. This dilemma, coupled with the resulting lack of anonymity, can dissuade victims from coming forward to seek help from service providers in sparsely populated areas. They note that this is exacerbated when coupled with distrust of social agencies and higher acceptance of IPV in remote regions. Victims who are geographically isolated face the additional burden of traveling to a service provider to begin with; a lack of infrastructure such as public transportation can further complicate this.

Small Town Solutions to a Widespread Problem

Although this violence is ubiquitous, it is easier to address in larger jurisdictions with more resources. Yet justice requires community members to work together to find solutions to the challenges to reporting in rural and remote jurisdictions. One idea shared by Petersson and Larsson is that victims seek social service support from a neighboring municipality to minimize confidentiality concerns. We can imagine other ideas that include remote reporting options, online access to counseling services, and other methods to connect with service providers in jurisdictions with similar small-town dynamics.

Regardless of geographic region, zip code, or population density, community members should invest time to know one another. Neighborhood watch programs don’t work unless neighbors are watching. Proactive collaboration creates the enhanced ability to spot red flags early, say something when we see something, and promote community safety for everyone.
